summary:
Vanuatu never criminalised same-sex conduct, and there is no documented pattern of anti-trans violence against visitors. That baseline sits alongside an official posture moving sharply against LGBT people: in November 2024 the Ministry of Justice and Community Services was directed to appoint a committee drafting a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion. National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 had targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, with V-Pride framed as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values. For a visibly trans or gender-nonconforming visitor, that framing is the operative risk signal, since it invites suspicion of advocacy or promotion rather than merely of private conduct.

Parliament amended the Marriage Act in November 2024 to define marriage as the union of a male and a female. Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed that same-sex marriages cannot be registered and that pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law. Couples travelling together should therefore expect no recognition of an existing marriage.

Legal gender recognition does not exist, so a visitor's documents will reflect the gender assigned at birth. There is no mechanism to alter markers before or during travel.

Protection machinery offers thin cover. A 2016 joint workshop by VPride Foundation and the Vanuatu Women's Centre established that same-sex partners receive no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must instead rely on penal-code routes. University of the South Pacific law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented a single prosecuted case of violence against lesbians and an LGBTI court presence that was near-invisible. VPride, founded in 2014, met opposition from church leaders, officials and chiefs at its founding, and a small community remains based in Port Vila.
tangentialFactors:
The November 2024 advocacy ban and the Marriage Act amendment belong to a wider Pacific pattern of legislative restriction, but Vanuatu's starting point differs from neighbouring jurisdictions that retain criminal statutes: conduct itself was never an offence, so enforcement risk attaches to visibility and speech rather than to private activity.

Kastom authority and church conservatism shape how rules are applied in practice. Chiefs as well as clergy and officials objected to VPride's founding, which indicates that social sanction can operate independently of the statute book, particularly outside Port Vila.

The near-absence of reported prosecutions reflects under-recognition and under-reporting rather than a finding of safety. Baseline crime concerns and limited service capacity apply as they would to any visitor, without an identified anti-trans violence pattern specific to travellers.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same gaps in protection that apply to visitors: same-sex partners are excluded from the Family Protection Act 2008 and must pursue complaints through penal-code provisions, a route documented as seldom used. Anita Jowitt's research found one prosecuted case of violence against lesbians and no meaningful LGBTI presence in the courts.

VPride Foundation, established in 2014 and operating from Port Vila, was opposed at founding by church leaders, officials and chiefs. Its joint human-rights work with the Vanuatu Women's Centre in 2016, funded by the Pacific Community, set out these legal gaps for the community itself.

No legal route to gender recognition exists for residents, and the 2024 Marriage Act amendment forecloses registration of same-sex marriages. The national policy on LGBTQIA+ advocacy, in draft as of November 2024, would bear directly on local organising and public statements rather than on visitors alone.
outOfScopeNotes:
The national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy was at the committee-drafting stage when last sourced, in November 2024; its final text, whether it has been adopted, and what penalties or enforcement mechanisms attach are unresolved and not stated in the available material.

No source in the inventory reports prosecutions, detentions or violence against trans people under the 2024 measures, so the practical enforcement picture for a trans visitor is unresolved rather than established as either active or dormant.

Whether the Family Protection Act 2008 exclusion has since been addressed, and whether any legal gender recognition process has opened, are not sourced either way. Port Vila is the only location where community presence is documented; conditions elsewhere are not covered.
